title: The Metaphors We Think With
question: Do we use metaphors to describe our thoughts, or do metaphors quietly build the thoughts themselves?
summary: Cognitive linguists argue that metaphor is not decoration on top of literal thought but the scaffolding of abstract reasoning itself, meaning the words we reach for when talking about time, arguments, or emotions may be shaping how we experience them.
content:
Say "prices are rising," "I'm feeling low," or "our relationship hit a wall," and you are not being poetic, you are using the ordinary machinery of language. In 1980, linguist George Lakoff and philosopher Mark Johnson published Metaphors We Live By, arguing that such phrases are not occasional flourishes but evidence of a deep structural fact: humans understand abstract domains almost entirely by mapping them onto concrete, bodily experience. We don't have direct cognitive access to concepts like time, argument, or affection, so we borrow structure from things we do have direct access to: space, objects, physical force, containers.

Conceptual Metaphor, Not Just Verbal Metaphor

Lakoff and Johnson's key distinction is between a figure of speech, which is a decorative choice, and a conceptual metaphor, which is a systematic mapping between two domains that shapes how we reason. "Argument is war" is a conceptual metaphor because it generates a whole family of consistent expressions: we defend a position, attack a claim, win or lose a debate, shoot down an idea. Notice we rarely describe arguments with a competing metaphor, such as "argument is a dance," where partners might build something collaborative and turns matter more than victory. Cultures that lack the war-based framing do sometimes use exactly that alternative, and their arguments reportedly unfold differently, with less emphasis on domination.

Time Is Space, Almost Everywhere

One of the most robust cross-linguistic patterns is that time gets described using spatial language: we move meetings forward, look back on the past, have a long way to go. English speakers tend to conceptualize time as moving horizontally, with the future ahead. Mandarin speakers use both horizontal and vertical time metaphors, with earlier events described as "up" and later ones as "down." Experiments by Lera Boroditsky found that briefly training English speakers to think in vertical time metaphors shifted how quickly they judged the order of events, suggesting the metaphor is not just describing an underlying spatial-free concept of time but actively participating in how that concept gets processed.

The Body as the Ultimate Source Domain

Why do so many metaphors, across unrelated languages, converge on the same handful of source domains: up/down, near/far, containers, forces, paths? The embodied cognition hypothesis holds that abstract reasoning is built out of recycled neural and conceptual machinery originally evolved for navigating physical space and manipulating objects. Happy is up and sad is down in a striking number of languages, plausibly because upright posture correlates with health and alertness while slumping correlates with illness and low energy. If this is right, abstract thought is not an independent faculty layered on top of perception; it is perception's software running on a slightly different set of inputs.

What Rides on This

The stakes are not purely academic. If metaphor genuinely structures reasoning rather than merely reporting it, then the metaphors embedded in policy language matter beyond style. Describing crime as a "virus" that "infects" a community versus a "beast" that must be "hunted" changes what solutions people find intuitive: containment and treatment in one frame, force and punishment in the other, according to studies by Paul Thibodeau and Lera Boroditsky. People rarely notice the metaphor doing this work; they experience their conclusion as following from the facts, when part of it was smuggled in through the framing.

perspectives.title: Cognitive Linguistics Perspective
perspectives.description: Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual metaphor theory treats systematic metaphor as direct evidence for how abstract concepts are mentally structured, not merely how they are expressed.

perspectives.title: Psycholinguistic Perspective
perspectives.description: Experimental work by researchers like Lera Boroditsky tests whether manipulating a metaphor changes measurable reasoning or judgment, moving the claim from armchair theory to testable prediction.

perspectives.title: Philosophical Perspective
perspectives.description: If thought is inherently metaphorical, this challenges the classical view of concepts as literal, metaphor-free representations, raising questions about whether any 'pure' abstract reasoning exists at all.

perspectives.title: Political Communication Perspective
perspectives.description: Framing research shows that the metaphors used in news coverage and policy debate measurably shift which solutions people find plausible, without their being aware persuasion has occurred.

openQuestions: If a culture's dominant metaphors changed deliberately, would its members' reasoning about that domain measurably change too?
Are there abstract concepts humans grasp without relying on any bodily or spatial metaphor at all?
How much of perceived political disagreement is actually disagreement over which metaphor to apply, rather than over facts?
Could an AI system trained without embodied sensory experience develop humanlike conceptual metaphors, or would its abstractions be structured entirely differently?
